items.title: Ocean Relief, Salinity, Temperature & Water Characteristics
items.body:
## Ocean relief (from coast to deep)

| Zone | Depth / character |
|---|---|
| Continental shelf | 0–200 m, gentle; richest **fishing grounds**, oil/gas |
| Continental slope | steep edge, shelf to deep floor |
| Continental rise | gentle apron of sediment |
| Abyssal plain | flat deep floor, 3,000–6,000 m |
| Trench | deepest (Mariana ~11 km) — at subduction zones |
| Mid-oceanic ridge | volcanic mountain chain at **divergent** boundaries |

## Characteristics of ocean water (syllabus wording)

- **Physical:** temperature, salinity, density, colour, waves.
- **Chemical:** dissolved gases (O₂, CO₂), nutrients, mineral salts.
- **Biological:** marine life — **plankton** (drifters), **nekton** (swimmers), **benthos** (bottom dwellers).

## Salinity

- Average salinity **≈ 35‰ (35 g/kg)**, dominated by NaCl.
- **Highest** in enclosed subtropical seas (Red Sea, Dead Sea ~332 g/L) due to high evaporation, no outlet; **lowest** near the equator (heavy rain) and poles (ice melt) and in the Baltic Sea.

## Temperature

- Decreases with **depth** and from the **equator to the poles**.
- **Thermocline** = layer of rapid temperature fall (~100–1,000 m) between warm surface and cold deep water.
keyPoints: Relief sequence: continental shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → trench/ridge.
Continental shelf (0–200 m) is the richest fishing ground and holds offshore oil/gas.
Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep ~10,935 m) is the deepest point on Earth; trenches form at subduction zones.
Ocean water characteristics: physical (temp, salinity, density), chemical (dissolved gases, salts), biological (plankton, nekton, benthos).
Average ocean salinity ≈ 35‰; highest in enclosed seas like the Dead Sea, lowest near equator/poles and the Baltic.
Thermocline separates warm surface water from cold deep water; temperature falls with depth and toward the poles.
items.source: NCERT — Fundamentals of Physical Geography (Oceans, Salinity, Temperature)

items.title: Ocean Currents, Waves & Tides
items.body:
## Ocean currents

- **Warm currents** flow from the equator poleward, usually along **western margins** of oceans; **cold currents** flow equatorward along **eastern margins**.
- Where warm and cold currents meet, nutrient upwelling creates the world's **great fishing grounds** (Grand Banks; Japan coast; Peru coast).

| Current | Type | Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| Gulf Stream | Warm | North Atlantic |
| Kuroshio | Warm | North-West Pacific |
| Humboldt (Peru) | Cold | South-East Pacific |
| Benguela | Cold | South-East Atlantic |
| Labrador / Canary | Cold | Atlantic |

## Movements of ocean water

- **Waves** — horizontal energy transfer driven by wind; water itself moves in circles.
- **Tides** — periodic rise/fall of sea level from the Moon's (and Sun's) gravity + centrifugal force.
  - **Spring tides**: new & full moon (Sun–Earth–Moon aligned) → highest range.
  - **Neap tides**: first & third quarter (Sun and Moon at right angles) → lowest range.
- Currents also moderate coastal **climate** — the Gulf Stream keeps NW Europe warm; cold currents cool adjacent coasts and cause fog.
keyPoints: Warm currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) flow poleward along western ocean margins; cold currents (Humboldt, Benguela, Labrador) flow equatorward along eastern margins.
Meeting of warm and cold currents (Grand Banks, Japan, Peru coast) creates the world's major fishing grounds.
Spring tides occur at new and full moon (alignment); neap tides at the first and third quarter (right angles).
Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity; the Sun's tidal effect is about 46% of the Moon's.
The Gulf Stream warms NW Europe, showing how currents regulate coastal climate.
items.source: NCERT — Fundamentals of Physical Geography (Ocean currents; Tides)

items.title: Coral Reefs — Types, Conditions & Bleaching
items.body:
## What corals need

- **Warm water** (~20–21°C or above) → tropical seas.
- **Shallow, clear, sediment-free** water so sunlight reaches the symbiotic algae (**zooxanthellae**).
- **Normal oceanic salinity**; corals die near large river mouths (fresh water, silt).

## Types of coral reefs

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fringing reef** | attached directly to the shore |
| **Barrier reef** | separated from the coast by a lagoon (e.g. Great Barrier Reef) |
| **Atoll** | ring-shaped reef enclosing a lagoon (common in the Pacific/Indian Ocean) |

## Coral bleaching

- Caused by **rising sea temperature** and acidification, which make corals expel their zooxanthellae, turning white and often dying.
- In India, reefs occur in the **Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands**.
keyPoints: Corals require warm (~20°C+), shallow, clear, sediment-free water of normal salinity.
Three reef types: fringing (shore-attached), barrier (lagoon-separated), atoll (ring-shaped).
Coral bleaching is the loss of symbiotic zooxanthellae due to warming and acidification.
Indian coral reef sites: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar.

items.title: Marine Resources, Ocean Energy & Blue Economy
items.body:
## Marine resources

- **Biotic:** fisheries (continental shelves), seaweed, marine biodiversity.
- **Mineral:** **polymetallic (manganese) nodules** (Mn, Ni, Cu, Co) on abyssal plains; placer sands (monazite, ilmenite); common salt.
- **Energy:** **offshore oil & gas** (e.g. Mumbai High); gas hydrates.

## Ocean (renewable) energy

| Form | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Tidal energy** | rise/fall of tides in a barrage (potential: Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat, Sundarbans) |
| **Wave energy** | kinetic energy of waves |
| **OTEC** | temperature difference (~20°C) between warm surface and cold deep water |

## Blue Economy & EEZ

- **Blue Economy** = sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, jobs and ecosystem health (fisheries, shipping, tourism, energy, biotechnology).
- **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)** extends **200 nautical miles** from the baseline (UNCLOS); India's EEZ ≈ **2.37 million km²**, with exclusive resource rights.
keyPoints: Marine resources: fisheries, polymetallic nodules (Mn/Ni/Cu/Co), placer sands, offshore oil & gas (Mumbai High).
Ocean energy has three forms — tidal (barrage), wave and OTEC (temperature-difference).
India's tidal-energy potential is in the Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat and Sundarbans.
Blue Economy = sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, jobs and ecosystem health.
EEZ extends 200 nautical miles under UNCLOS; India's EEZ is about 2.37 million km².
items.source: Ministry of Earth Sciences; NCERT — Mineral and Energy Resources; UNCLOS

items.title: Deep Ocean Mission & Samudrayaan
items.body:
## Deep Ocean Mission (DOM)

- Launched in **2021** by the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)** to explore the deep ocean for resources and develop deep-sea technology; supports India's Blue Economy vision.
- A multi-year programme with **six components**, including deep-sea mining & manned submersible, ocean climate services, marine biodiversity, deep-ocean survey, energy/fresh-water from the ocean, and an advanced marine-station for ocean biology.

## Samudrayaan

- India's **first manned deep-ocean mission**, sending **three persons to 6,000 m** in the indigenous submersible **MATSYA-6000**, built by the **National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai**.
- Targets exploration of **deep-sea minerals (polymetallic nodules)** and biodiversity in the **Central Indian Ocean Basin**, where India holds an International Seabed Authority exploration site.
- Makes India part of a small group of nations with crewed deep-submergence capability.
keyPoints: Deep Ocean Mission was launched in 2021 under the Ministry of Earth Sciences to explore deep-sea resources and technology.
It has six components spanning deep-sea mining, manned submersible, ocean climate services, biodiversity, ocean energy/fresh water and an ocean-biology station.
Samudrayaan is India's first manned deep-ocean mission — three persons to 6,000 m in the submersible MATSYA-6000.
MATSYA-6000 is built by NIOT, Chennai; targets polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin.
Deep Ocean Mission directly supports India's Blue Economy goals.
items.source: Ministry of Earth Sciences / NIOT — Deep Ocean Mission

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Coast, Fisheries & Marine Hazards
items.body:
## Andhra Pradesh coast

- Coastline **~974 km — the longest on India's east coast** and second-longest among Indian states after Gujarat.
- **Ports:** **Visakhapatnam** (the only major/Union port); non-major ports include **Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Machilipatnam**.
- The **Godavari and Krishna deltas** create rich estuarine and marine fishing zones; AP is a **national leader in fisheries and shrimp/aquaculture exports** (via MPEDA).

## Marine & coastal hazards

| Hazard | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Tsunami** | undersea earthquake (2004: Sumatra, Mw ~9.1) |
| **Storm surge** | wind-driven sea rise during cyclones (Bay of Bengal) |
| **Coastal flooding / erosion** | surge + delta low-lying land |

## Mitigation & marine pollution

- **INCOIS (Hyderabad)** runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (since 2007).
- Marine pollution: plastics, oil spills, sewage/nutrients (eutrophication), industrial effluents — tackled through **CRZ rules, MARPOL compliance and clean-coast (Swachh Sagar) drives**.
keyPoints: AP's coastline is ~974 km — the longest on India's east coast (2nd in India after Gujarat).
Visakhapatnam is AP's only major port; Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Machilipatnam are key non-major ports.
AP is a national leader in fisheries and shrimp/aquaculture exports, aided by the Godavari and Krishna deltas.
The 2004 tsunami (Sumatra earthquake) hit the AP coast; storm surges and coastal flooding are cyclone-driven hazards.
INCOIS, Hyderabad runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre; marine pollution is managed via CRZ rules and clean-coast drives.
items.source: AP State Portal; Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways; MPEDA; INCOIS

items.title: High-yield Facts — Counter Current, Chandipur, OMT & Water Distribution
items.body:
## Equatorial Counter Current

- The trade-wind-driven **North and South Equatorial Currents** flow **west** and **pile water up on the western side** of the ocean.
- This water flows back **eastward** along the calm equatorial trough as the **Equatorial Counter Current** (convergence, not wind).

## Chandipur 'vanishing sea'

- At **Chandipur (Odisha)** the sea recedes up to ~5 km twice a day at low tide, exposing the floor — an exceptional tidal range on a very gentle shore.

## Ocean Mean Temperature (OMT) — monsoon predictor

- **OMT** = ocean heat content down to the **26°C isotherm** (~129 m) in the **south-western Indian Ocean**, measured **January-March**.
- Being more stable than surface temperature, the **Jan-Mar OMT predicts** whether the monsoon will be below or above the long-term mean.

## Global water distribution

| Store | Share |
|---|---|
| Oceans (saline) | ~97.3% |
| Ice caps & glaciers | largest **freshwater** store (~2%) |
| Groundwater | next largest freshwater store |
| Rivers & lakes | a tiny surface fraction |

- Freshwater hierarchy: **ice caps/glaciers > groundwater > surface (rivers/lakes)**.
keyPoints: The eastward Equatorial Counter Current arises from the convergence/piling-up of the North and South Equatorial Currents on the ocean's western side.
Chandipur (Odisha) is the 'vanishing sea' — the sea recedes a few km twice daily, exposing the floor.
OMT is ocean heat to the 26°C isotherm depth (~129 m) in the SW Indian Ocean, measured Jan-March.
The Jan-March OMT is a better predictor of monsoon rainfall than sea-surface temperature.
Water distribution: oceans ~97.3%; freshwater hierarchy is ice caps/glaciers > groundwater > rivers & lakes.
items.source: UPSC CSE Prelims 2013/2015/2017/2020/2021; NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography; IITM Pune
